Masculinity

Project 35 · a project, not a verdict · index

Scope. This project treats masculinity as a set of historical answers to one question: what is a man for? The answers change by century and by class, they are enforced more by other men than by women, and most of them were written down by people who were worried the current answer was failing. The project’s output is a map of those answers, a short list of the models scholars use to sort them, and a plan for the parts of this repo that already touch the subject.

1. Six answers, in order

WhenWordA man is forEnforced byFailure looks like
Homeric Greecearetē, excellencewinning in front of witnessesother warriors, the poetParis: pretty, beloved, and in the tent
Classical Athensandreia, courageholding the line in the phalanx, speaking in the assemblythe citythe “soft” man, the one who cannot govern himself
Republican Romevirtusservice to the republic, self-commandthe censors, the familyluxury, Greek habits, weeping in public
Medieval Europechivalryfighting for a lord and protecting the weak, in theorythe order, the church, the romancethe coward and the churl, in different directions
Victorian Britainmanlinesswork, restraint, providing, the stiff upper lipthe public school, the firmthe idler, the dandy, the nervous man
Twentieth centurymasculinitythe breadwinner, then the self-made man, then the question itselfadvertising, the workplace, other menthe “crisis of masculinity”, declared roughly every twenty years since 1890

Two things are constant across the rows. The standard is always measured against other men, and the anxiety that the standard is slipping is as old as the standard. Roman moralists complained about soft young men in the second century BC; the phrase “crisis of masculinity” has appeared in print in every decade since the 1890s.

2. Four models for sorting the answers

Hegemonic masculinity (Connell, 1987–2005)

In any society one form of masculinity is dominant, and other forms — subordinated, complicit, marginalised — are ranked against it. The dominant form is rarely the most common; it is the most honoured. Useful because it explains why most men do not fit the standard they enforce.

Precarious manhood (Vandello and Bosson, 2008)

Manhood, unlike womanhood, is treated as earned and losable: it must be proven repeatedly and can be taken away by a single failure. Explains the disproportionate reaction to small challenges.

The man box (Kivel; Promundo, 2017)

A survey instrument: self-sufficiency, toughness, attractiveness, rigid roles, heterosexuality, hypersexuality, aggression. Men who score high report more violence and worse mental health; the box is bad for the men inside it.

Caring masculinities (Elliott, 2016)

The proposal that the answer to “what is a man for” can be care without ceasing to be masculine. The least tested of the four and the one with the most policy behind it.

3. What the evidence supports, briefly

  • Men die earlier in almost every country, die by suicide at roughly three to four times the rate of women in most of the West, and are the large majority of both perpetrators and victims of homicide. These are the plain numbers any model has to explain.
  • Boys now trail girls in schooling in most rich countries, and the gap widens with each level. Reeves’ Of Boys and Men (2022) is the accessible summary.
  • The traits usually filed under masculinity — risk tolerance, physical aggression, interest in things over people — show real average sex differences, with very large overlap. The differences are real and small; the stereotypes are large and coarse.
  • Men’s friendships thin out with age more than women’s, and loneliness in middle-aged men is the strongest single predictor the surveys have found for the bad outcomes above.

4. Plan for this repo

The ship already has three places where the subject lives without saying so. The session list includes Explore Hellenistic society from male perspective and its companion from the female one. The archetype templates have an officeholder. The warlock dossier (project 33) files scholars and teachers under a word that was used against women in exactly the opposite way. The plan:

  1. Add a templates-manhood/ directory with one JSON per answer in section 1, same shape as templates-warlock/: id, order, name, where, when, was, why. Six files to start.
  2. Give each archetype a standard field naming which answer it is measured against, so the archetype page can show it.
  3. Reuse the Hellenistic session pair as the first worked example: the same city, two perspectives, one page each, generated from the same data.
  4. Keep the caricature satire (project 36) separate and labelled, so nobody mistakes it for section 3.

5. What this project declines to do

It does not rank the six answers, does not pick a side in the current argument about whether the word should be rescued or retired, and does not offer advice. Those are all real questions; they are not this project’s, and a page that answered them would be read as a position rather than as a map.
